analysis.one_liner: Bans doctors from billing patients for lab, imaging, and therapy services they don't perform themselves.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee from April 1995 until the Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal to send a bill for lab tests, X-rays and other imaging, medical equipment, or physical therapy to anyone other than the patient, with exceptions for family members, insurers, HMOs, hospitals, and similar payers. Its core rule is aimed at doctors who refer patients to labs or imaging facilities they own or profit from: a doctor could only bill the patient for such services if the doctor, their group practice, or their supervised employees actually performed the service. It would not apply to services billed through Medicare, which is already covered by a separate federal self-referral law.
analysis.who_benefits: Privately insured and uninsured patients, who would no longer receive bills for tests and scans ordered by doctors with a financial stake in the facility performing them; insurers and employers, who would pay fewer claims for marked-up ancillary services; and patients referred out by their doctor, who would keep choice over where to get a test instead of being steered to the doctor's own facility.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Privately insured patients and health insurers

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful for a physician to bill a patient for ancillary services — clinical lab work, diagnostic X-rays and imaging including CT and MRI, other diagnostic tests, durable medical equipment, and physical therapy — unless the services were furnished personally by the referring doctor, a member of the same group practice, or supervised employees of that practice [S2] [S3].

States the purpose directly: to eliminate the incentives that lead to increased prices and utilization of clinical laboratory diagnostic testing and other ancillary health services — the financial incentive created when the doctor referring the test also profits from it [S3].

Backs the rule with teeth: no payment for services billed in violation, mandatory refunds of amounts improperly collected, civil fines up to $5,000 per repeated improper claim, and possible suspension or revocation of a lab's federal certification or exclusion from Medicare and state health programs [S2] [S3].
A patient would keep the freedom to take a doctor's order to any lab or imaging center, rather than being billed for services funneled to a facility the referring doctor owns [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Physicians with ownership stakes in outside labs, imaging centers, equipment suppliers, and physical therapy operations, who would lose the ability to profit from services they refer but do not perform, and would face fines, refunds, and possible exclusion from Medicare for repeated violations. Some independent ancillary providers could also lose business if they had relied on billing arrangements with physicians.
analysis.who_pays_short: Doctors with stakes in labs and imaging centers

drawbacks.text: The ban is broad and relies on many exceptions — for family members, designated payors, HMOs, hospitals, employers, government agencies, confidentiality-sensitive testing, research, and any other entity the Secretary approves — so the line between legal and illegal billing would depend heavily on regulations the Secretary had to write by mid-1997 [S3].

The bill does not cover services billable under Medicare, so the main financial-incentive rule applies only to the private-pay and private-insurance market, leaving a patchwork where the same conduct is governed differently by program [S2] [S3].

Good-faith objections from the medical community would center on the compliance burden: group practices would have to document supervision of staff performing ancillary services, and honest billing mistakes could trigger refunds and civil penalties, costs that would fall on small practices as well as on genuinely conflicted ones [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and targeted: it removes a documented conflict of interest in which the doctor who orders a test profits from the bill, which tends to raise prices and utilization for patients and insurers outside Medicare. The costs are administrative — compliance and documentation for physician practices — and the main design weakness is the Medicare carve-out plus the Secretary-approved exceptions, which leave the rule narrower and more complicated than a clean self-referral ban. On balance, the consumer protections outweigh the compliance burden, but the bill as written would have required substantial regulation to work in practice.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Commerce Committee and then to its Health and Environment subcommittee in April 1995, and nothing further ever happened to it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Fred Upton introduced the bill on April 6, 1995, joined by Rep. Brown of Ohio, and it was referred to the House Committee on Commerce the same day [S1] [S3] [S5].

On April 24, 1995, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment, and the action record shows no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action for the rest of the 104th Congress [S5].
The bill had two cosponsors, one Democrat and one Republican, and never advanced past the subcommittee before the Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Physicians who owned or profited from labs, imaging centers, equipment suppliers, and therapy operations kept their existing billing arrangements, because the restriction was never enacted. Patients and insurers outside Medicare continued to bear the cost of ancillary services ordered by doctors with a financial stake in them.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Republican and cosponsored by one Democrat and one Republican, but with only two cosponsors and no recorded votes, the record does not show a partisan split on the merits; it simply died without action.

industries.industry: Physician-owned ancillary services (labs, imaging centers, DME suppliers, physical therapy)
industries.note: Doctors who refer patients to facilities they own or profit from would lose the ability to bill patients for services they do not personally perform. This profit depends on patients paying marked-up prices for services steered to the doctor's own facility, so its interest runs against the patient's.

industries.industry: Independent clinical laboratories and imaging providers
industries.note: With doctors barred from billing for referred ancillary services, patients would take orders to independent labs and imaging centers, increasing their business. Patients would benefit from choice and from the removal of self-referral markups.

industries.industry: Health insurers and employer health plans
industries.note: Insurers and self-insured employers would pay fewer claims for ancillary services billed with a self-referral markup, lowering premiums and benefit costs. The bill expressly allows billing to designated payors and HMOs for actual services rendered.

industries.industry: Medicare (federal program) and its participating providers
industries.note: The bill exempts services billable under Medicare, since a separate federal law already restricts self-referral there. Medicare providers are spared the new rules, but the carve-out leaves a split system between Medicare and private-pay patients.
